This initial size is comparable to the minimal dimensions observed among other members of the Sididae family, although it marks the start of a pronounced growth trajectory. Within a couple of days, the newly released juvenile begins filter feeding on ambient phytoplankton, transitioning rapidly from reliance on internal resources to active exogenous nutrition. This early period is energetically intensive, and the interval between release from the brood chamber and the commencement of independent feeding is brief. At a constant water temperature maintained in laboratory cultures, the age at birth was recorded as 2.1 days [ab = 2.1 days], a value that underscores the rapid developmental pace characteristic of this cladoceran under optimal thermal conditions. This abbreviated embryonic period allows for a quick generation turnover, which is a common life-history strategy among small-bodied zooplankton inhabiting ephemeral or highly productive freshwater habitats.

Juveniles undergo a series of molts, each instar yielding a stepwise increase in carapace length. The progression toward reproductive competence is marked by the attainment of a specific body dimension, with puberty being reached when individuals measure 0.090 cm [Lp = 0.090 cm] in total length. This threshold size is reached relatively quickly after birth, with the time since birth at puberty occurring after 2.1 days since birth [tp = 2.1 days since birth] when experiments are conducted at a stable temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C]. The synchronization of somatic growth with developmental milestones is a critical feature of the species' life cycle, ensuring that individuals do not divert energy toward gamete production before they have achieved a sufficient structural frame to support brooding. Across the genus Latonopsis, such a precise size-at-maturity relationship is thought to be an adaptation to variable food availability, allowing females to delay reproduction if resources are scarce without compromising eventual fecundity.

Once females surpass the pubertal size threshold, they continue to grow until they approach an asymptotic body dimension. The ultimate total length recorded for this species is 0.165 cm [Li = 0.165 cm], a size that represents the maximum carapace length attained by fully mature adults under favorable laboratory conditions. At this terminal size, the dry weight of a reproductively active female is considerable given the small stature of the animal, with an ultimate dry weight of 53 micrograms . This mass reflects not only the structural components of the exoskeleton but also the substantial lipid reserves and developing embryos carried within the brood pouch. The relationship between length and mass in L. australis is consistent with allometric scaling patterns observed across the Cladocera, where a cubic function typically describes the volume-to-mass conversion. Compared to congeners with a more elongated body form, L. australis exhibits a slightly stockier build, which may confer advantages in terms of buoyancy and resistance to predation by tactile invertebrate predators.

Reproductive output in Latonopsis australis is tightly linked to the thermal regime of the water column. The combination of a moderately large clutch size with a fast instar turnover allows females to sustain a high daily output of offspring during their peak reproductive window. This strategy is energetically demanding and requires a consistent supply of high-quality algal food to maintain lipid reserves. Field surveys in subtropical water bodies suggest that such high rates are achieved only during bloom periods when phytoplankton density is elevated, with natural populations often falling short of this laboratory-determined maximum due to resource limitation and the presence of invertebrate predators.

The species exhibits a relatively compressed life span when maintained at elevated temperatures. At 29 °C [T = 29 °C], the maximum longevity recorded for adult females is 46 days [am = 46 days], a duration that encompasses the entire period from release from the brood chamber to natural senescence. The final phase of life is characterized by a cessation of molting and a decline in feeding activity, culminating in physiological death. This post-reproductive interval is brief, suggesting that reproductive senescence and somatic death are closely coupled in this species, with little to no extended post-reproductive survival. The ability to complete the entire life cycle in under seven weeks allows L. australis to colonize temporary ponds and shallow littoral zones that may dry out seasonally.
